At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Models that incorporate large-scale cosmic structure and account for the scattering of cosmic rays by magnetic fields (with a strength of 1.68 μG) are compatible with our results. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. The series nature of these metric formulas may be considered as an issue for conventional quantum mechanics since it implies infinite waves' energy states existence. Nevertheless, the issue can be resolved by introducing a maximum possible wave's energy, which corresponds to the deformation of usual special relativity. This deformation leads to a limit on wave lengths' minimization, influencing the observable universe's size. Furthermore, the study reveals that the deformed quantum mechanics ensures the stability of the hydrogen-like atom with the charge distribution restricted to a certain area. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate these errors, a weighted DFE method was employed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This approach was successfully validated through a field trial over the aforementioned 18.8km underwater cable, with the best-performing configuration demonstrating a reduced BER of 8.57x10^-5 at a 72Gbit/s data rate following the 18.8km distance, indicating that the weighted DFE-MLSE method can be an effective technique for compensating chromatic dispersion and mitigating burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. The worst-performed configuration of this technique however experienced a much higher BER of 3.57x10^-3 at the same data rate following the same distance, implying future potential for further optimization of this technique, and ultimately suggesting that it holds great promise for increasing the spectral efficiency of future submarine communications systems, potentially supporting up to 100Gbit/s data rates over the 18.8km underwater cable. The limitations of this study were the use of a single-span transmission system and the absence of four-wave mixing, factors that typically affect real-world communications systems. To more accurately reflect these conditions, a future study should incorporate a 96Gbit/s, four-wave mixing affected signal in a two-span transmission system. Additionally, the marine conditions that induced the burst errors in this study were artificially created, hence future studies should investigate the effects of natural marine conditions on fiber-optic communications systems. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse process is shown to be sound when ALBA correspondence holds, and we explore potential applications of this inverse approach in the context of the Sahlqvist correspondence and the Iteration Operator. Our results demonstrate that this inverse strategy provides a compelling framework that can capture and systematize a wide range of correspondence theories and related concepts, such as the algebraic and order-theoretic properties essential for correspondence to hold. Furthermore, this framework facilitates a straightforward implementation of ALBA-based correspondence for monodic logics and sets of formulas, and an order-theoretic generalization of the I-Operator that is compatible with a broader class of semantical frameworks. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Theoretical findings of this research have implications on the management of inconsistent data and address an open question regarding the consistency of query answers. Finally, we outline an extension of this research to handle cycle-free dependency chains and an intriguing problem of data quality assessment. The concepts developed in this research are an important step toward a more comprehensive theory on the management of inconsistent data and have significant implications on data quality assessment and query validation. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Furthermore, rerelevant performance figures are being refocused towards the detector's overall performance rather than individual components' characteristics. Moreover, the incorporation of particle flow analysis performance markers will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the detector's capabilities. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondences with the highest confidence are selected from the output of the projection grouping module, and a robust correspondence filter is proposed to enhance the correspondence quality before being used for final pose estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework not only surpasses the performance of direct methods but also significantly outperforms the current two-stage pipeline baselines. Furthermore, our framework's flexibility allows for the integration of additional cues such as light fields or normed 3D vectors, thereby achieving superior performance in the Oxford and IFT3D datasets. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results show that FPG yields up to 200% performance gains compared to the attack-free case and 50% performance gains compared to an uncorrupted setting at the $\epsilon=0.2$ corruption level. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. This method has been found to be robust in various clinical settings and is more straightforward for clinical practitioners to incorporate into the clinical workflow. Furthermore, this study's findings may also be applicable to other tumor segmentation tasks in CT scans. This study's results were also presented at the Scientific Meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) in 2019. Additionally, our model has been found to perform well on the publicly available segmentation challenges, achieving the best overall score in the 2016 MICCAI challenge and a score greater than 0.75 in 11 out of 13 other challenges. This model has been incorporated into a software library called Highly Accurate Segmentation Software (HASS) that can be downloaded from https://github.com/MedPlore/HASS. This library provides a range of high-accuracy segmentation algorithms for various organs and tumors that can be easily integrated into clinical workflows. This has implications for cancer diagnosis and treatment, which heavily relies on accurate imaging

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. Ensemble-based material balance calculations are incorporated into a non-linear radial e-PDF method to achieve this goal.  The approach uses an ensemble of radial probability density functions, each representing a possible formation configuration based on well and formation properties.  Following material balance calculations, these functions are transformed into radial e-PDFs, which are then updated using ensemble-based techniques to reflect the effects of well and formation interactions.  This results in refined ensembles that account for the uncertainties associated with well logging tools and their interpretations.  The approach is validated using synthetic and real well log data from sandstone and carbonate reservoirs.  The proposed method demonstrates its capability to handle the uncertainties associated with well logging tools and their interpretations, and the results show that it complies with the physical properties of the formation.  The method also highlights the importance of well logging data quality, particularly the impact of resistivity tools on geosteering.  The method is found to be more accurate than conventional methods, and it is suitable for real-time implementation.  The approach is also compatible with the industry-standard geosteering software, Petrosys.  The method can be used to generate multiple possible well trajectories, consider the effects of wellbore storage, and validate the formation evaluations, The method is currently being tested and integrated into the geosteering system of a major oil and gas company. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our method achieves comparable performance to sequence labeling-based approaches while being more versatile in modeling corpus-level statistics and phenomena. Our model has also been applied in real-world applications, detailed in https://github.com/ASAI-HK/real-world-applications. Our proposed method has been adopted by the University of Washington and the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and has been incorporated into the Stanford CoreNLP tool. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, to facilitate real-world applications, we have incorporated a new method for managing coordinate boundaries, thereby enabling the location of mobile nodes within a real-world environment. Experimental findings reveal that location estimation can be accurate to within 7.5 cm when certain parameters are optimized. Additionally, comparisons with other location estimation methods, such as Horus and Mint, have shown our approach yields a significantly lower error rate. The design and execution of this project also highlight the importance of considering all technologies operating within a particular frequency range when developing location estimation algorithms.  To this end, we propose the term "same technology interference" (STI) and explore its application in the context of wireless sensor networks.  A new method for calculating the distance between nodes, known as the "minimum STI distance", is also presented.  This approach takes into account the effects of interference between different hardware components, such as the differences in radio frequencies and operating systems used by different devices. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By investing in code-mixing NLP, there are potential gains to be made, especially when other low-resource language combinations are involved. To facilitate progress, we propose an open-access code-mixing dataset named Codemix-1B, comprising 1 billion word pairs available for research use. Codemix-1B can serve as a starting point for further advancements in code-mixing NLP. The dataset Codemix-1B along with additional information can be found at https://codemix-nlp.org/. This work is a step forward in addressing the numerous challenges and considerations facing multilingual societies, and future developments in code-mixing NLP are sure to bring numerous benefits and opportunities for growth. This initiative marks the beginning of a new code-mixing NLP community, and the Codemix-NLP workshop is an open invitation to all interested researchers and practitioners to join and contribute to the development of code-mixing NLP systems. The Codemix-NLP workshop will provide a forum for presenting research, exchanging ideas, and exploring collaboration opportunities and potential sources of funding in this emerging and promising field of NLP. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, automatic description systems can be compared to each other, or evaluation metrics tailored to the specific application or scenario can be developed. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Conversely, in areas with a strong sense of community and social responsibility, misinformation dissemination was reduced, but so was the exposure to news in general. Our findings reveal that The Big Sort may contribute substantially to the widespread circulation of misinformation, suggest targeting cultural interventions in areas with low social capital, and highlight the necessity of considering geographical sorting when evaluating online misinformation studies. Additionally, we found that mitigating the spread of misinformation in some areas may require collaborating with local news outlets to increase news exposure. Nevertheless, this interpretation comes with the limitation that it might not be universally applicable, and the role of The Big Sort may vary across different geographic areas. Consequently, our results highlight the value of incorporating cultural and historical context in the study of online misinformation phenomena. Furthermore, we show that observing users' behavior in online platforms can serve as a leading indicator of potential misinformation dissemination in those areas, which may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying factors behind the spread of misinformation. Ultimately, our analysis demonstrates that The Big Sort has a lasting impact on the social dynamics of online communities and shapes the circulation of misinformation among Reddit users in the United States. 

Finally, we provide a numerical representation of the variability of misinformation dissemination across different geographic areas, showing that some areas have triple the rate of dissemination when compared to others, and highlight the limitations of existing studies due to their failure to account for The Big Sort. We also emphasize the importance of considering the cultural and historical context in the study of online misinformation, and the value of incorporating historical data in the analysis of dynamic phenomena. Moreover, we highlight the necessity of targeting local interventions in areas with low social capital, and the importance of collaborating with local news outlets to increase news exposure in areas with strong community norms

We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. As a result, the model can efficiently detect anomalies in various settings, demonstrating that human-in-the-loop machine learning can be a robust and effective solution. Furthermore, our method highlights the potential for human-machine collaboration to address complex issues, paving the way for the development of more sophisticated human-in-the-loop machine learning systems. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we observed evidence of photonic-quantum interface capability through the measurement of stable T center-based photon collection. These breakthroughs bring us closer to developing efficient, controllable, and reliable photonic quantum devices. Due to the widespread use of SOI technology, our approach offers a versatile platform for the development of complex photonic quantum technologies. Additionally, our research showcases the capabilities of optical communications within the same wavelength range used for communication, promoting the exploration of novel applications in quantum physics. Furthermore, we propose that combined efforts from experimental and theoretical research are essential for driving innovation and technological advancement in the quantum era. In conclusion, we present our findings in the context of recent breakthroughs in quantum research, highlighting the unique features of SOI-based T centers and the progress made towards developing quantum communication technologies. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. We make key contributions by applying a novel embedding methodology to real-world large-scale encyclopedic datasets and developing an efficient entity recommendation framework that balances sophistication and practicality for seamless deployment. The technical feasibility and effectiveness of this approach were validated through both rigorous experimentation and actual deployment. We release our implementation and methodology in detail for the broader research community to build upon. Historically, both graph-based methods and traditional collaborative filtering techniques have been explored for entity recommendations in Wikipedia. Nevertheless, previous Wikipedia-based entity recommendation approaches suffered from limited coverage and low quality, hindering the effectiveness of these methods. To address these challenges, our team developed a more comprehensive and higher-quality Wikipedia knowledge graph used for entity recommendations. This expanded knowledge graph covers 2 million entities and 2.5 billion relationships across 32 languages. Nonetheless, recommending entities within this vast graph poses a significant challenge. To overcome this difficulty, we introduced the concept of a Wikipedia-based "neighborhood". This neighborhood represents a distinct category or domain within the overall Wikipedia structure. We established a systematic method to divide the Wikipedia graph into such neighborhoods. Our approach ensures that each neighborhood exhibits a unique topic or domain and features a distinct hierarchy. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled structure of these contexts, an aspect that current static techniques fail to capture. We illustrate the challenges involved in classifying company names using word2vec embeddings and the limitations of existing methods, suggesting that successful classification would benefit from more sophisticated techniques, such as spherical spiral embedding analysis, and from incorporating temporal and analogies constraints. Our study provides a comprehensive examination of the capabilities and limitations of word2vec models, revealing their ability to capture the structure of frequentist synonyms, but also their inability to grasp antonyms and context-dependent polarities. We demonstrate the importance of considering the underlying statistical structure of these models, highlighting the challenges involved in applying them to challenging domains like finance, and the benefits of employing more advanced techniques, such as SPSE. Our results also underscore the value of incorporating temporal and analogies constraints in the embedding generation process, a feature that we introduce as a method constraint, suitable for any type of embedding framework. We anticipate that our results will prompt a critical reevaluation of the word2vec model, particularly its widespread use in finance, and the incorporation of temporal and analogies constraints in the embedding generation process. Our study sets the stage for a more thorough examination of other types of neural network-based embedding models, an area that we aim to explore in depth in our future research.

Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. The method's utility is demonstrated through the solution of a paradigmatic sentence involving both lexical and derivational ambiguity from Dowty's Chaircasting scenario. The proposed method provides a more sophisticated and principled approach to the interpretation of unary modalities than the existing category-theoretic methods and our case study highlights its potential in handling the expressiveness of formal type systems aligned with the compositional interpretation framework. The method's potential extension to other type systems and the Spin DMC framework are also discussed. The proposed approach may also offer a solution to the issue of over-distributionalisation encountered in previous implementations of the Lambek Calculus and our results suggest that the Spin DMC framework provides a more robust approach to the interpretation of the Lambek Calculus than the vectorial interpretation method. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research provides the first systematic answer to whether multiagent learning algorithms can efficiently discover rationalizable and potentially equilibrium behavior under bandit feedback. It does so by developing an general framework for testing whether particular action profiles satisfy particular criteria using the associated query complexity. This framework facilitates the derivation of a general lower bound for problem parameters including the number of players. This research raises another question regarding the efficacy of learning algorithms when the game changes over time. This change is captured by the recently introduced concept of Dynamic Correlated Equilibria (DCE). This paper proposes an efficient general-purpose algorithm to discover a DCE action profile, providing a solution to the second problem posed earlier. This algorithm is essentially an extension of the previous ones but is underpinned by a novel filtering approach that leverages the current state of the art in both the online learning and the bandit learning contexts. This results in an enhanced polynomial sample complexity that matches the static learning counterpart, thus demonstrating the insensitivity of efficient learning to stochastic game transitions. This research is an adaptation of two prior studies from 2020 and 2021 on the development of efficient algorithms in single-agent learning contexts. Notably, the previous results on learning equilibria and rationalizable behavior in multiplayer games were recently outperformed in terms of the achieved sample complexity at the same Neuro-ICML 2021 conference. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, we prove that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a shrinking Cotton soliton occurs when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field, resulting in a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Additionally, we establish that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a contracting Cotton soliton emerges when the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Moreover, we prove that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a conformally steady Cotton soliton occurs when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field, resulting in a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. This paper presents an implementation of an automated theory pipeline that can combine the predictions for various processes directly from PDF codes like xQCD and DGLAP tools like HOPES and DVEL, also providing basic phenomenological applications at the level of processes and including recommendations for further development in line with potential developments in research groups. This theory pipeline has been utilized to generate outputs for the working groups within the 2022 "Connect Theory Tools and Data" workshop. Given its modular design, this project can serve as a starting point for developing a professional framework that can seamlessly integrate theoretical predictions for PDF fitting, fitting that form the basis of numerous phenomenological studies in particle physics. This approach has implications for the broader particle physics community, highlighting the significance of open-data and open-code policies, as well as the value derived from collaborative efforts between research groups. This initiative can also be seen as an example of a community project that promotes the development of suitable tools for integrating experimental and theoretical data, in line with the principles of open science. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. The code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Prashant-Singh-Kashyap/VRER. The method's parameters are also provided to guide other researchers in the field. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources, our results reveal the combined effects of band back-bending and band folding resulting in a flat band at the center of the Brillouin zone. Moreover, our data directly demonstrates the band folding in both superconducting and normal states around the zone center, allowing for correct assignment of the hole-like bands. Near the zone corner, our results show an electron-like and M-shaped band in both states and a superconducting gap size around the zone corner ($\sim$5.5 meV), contradicting previous findings. These outcomes reveal a new gap structure around the zone corner, resolve prominent controversies and offer novel perspectives to analyze and understand the mechanism behind superconductivity in iron-based superconductors. 
  (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ ultimately presents an intriguing case where the superconducting gap size may hold the answer to explain the discrepancy between ARPES and specific heat measurements.

  Furthermore, our findings suggest that the superconducting gap structure around the zone corner may serve as an important clue for solving the general puzzle of how to explain the growth of superconducting gap size from the zone corner to the electron-like band around the zone corner in various iron-based superconductors.

Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Furthermore, our measurements of the nuclear magnetic moment correlation time fail to exhibit the expected temperature dependence predicted by the slow-re recovering component, leading us to consider alternative explanations. We propose that the slow-recovering component may arise from interactions between LaNiO$_3$ layers rather than intra-layer interactions. Consequently, our findings provide further evidence for the interfacial coupling in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices playing a pivotal role in governing the metallic state of the LaNiO$_3$ layers. Additionally, we highlight that the spin dynamics within these systems is more intricate than commonly assumed, refuting the classification as a correlated metallic state in the same vein as stripe phase or heavy fermion materials. Lastly, we suggest that adjusting the coupling between LaNiO$_3$ layers via tensile strain or hydrostatic pressure may further refine our understanding of the spin dynamics within these systems.... Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We also show that the latter can be interpreted through the lens of the Riemann-Hilbert problem, providing an alternative perspective on the Dyson model's connections to analytic functions. Additionally, we explore the statistics of the imaginary part of the boundary of the evolving domain, demonstrating that it follows the multiple SLE path. This result provides a practical path for implementing and numerically solving these processes using existing multiple SLE software. Finally, we extend Miller and Sheffield's definition of an imaginary surface to encompass these new developments. In certain two-dimensional spin models with significant site-to-site interactions, like the extended-Hubbard and XXZ models, robust, self-organizing clusters are observed at adjacent sites. These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems featuring near-neighbor clusterization, an intertwined interplay unfolds as these clusters perform an 'interactive walk,' giving rise to multiple temporal dynamics. Such behavior holds universally across any dimension; however, its impact is particularly noticeable in lower dimensions due to increased spatial correlations. A more detailed examination of these processes can be achieved through a localized, real-space approach that leverages effective Hamiltonians. This methodology enables the exploration of fundamental properties, like the scattering of sound waves, as predicted by a dynamical clusterization Hamiltonian. This framework is particularly valuable for understanding how two-dimensional systems evolve when put under external stress, given that such stress often results in a more efficient creation of clusters over time. A key observation made in this study finds that even when clusterization is robust, as seen in models like the one-dimensional Mott insulator, the Mott-Hubbard gap can be closed by incorporating short-range three-body forces, an effect that holds true for any dimension. This prediction positions this study as a foundation for exploring more complex, higher-dimensional systems that feature clusters that walk in an interacting manner. This work is a collaboration between Rice University, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Santa Barbara, the University of Innsbruck, the University of Geneva, the University of Nottingham, and the University of Oxford. It is supported by the Welch Foundation, the NSF-MRSEC, the NSF-CAREER, the NSF-DMR, the Swiss National Science Foundation, and the Austrian Science Fund. The theoretical predictions made in this study have been verified by experimental measurements conducted at Rice University. The experimental techniques used involved creating a two-dimensional lattice of atoms through the laser cooling of atomic gases in optical-lattice setups, manipulating inter-site interactions via photoassociation, and controlling the movement of these clusters with intensity patterns in the laser. A new method for producing sound waves in these systems has been developed, and a new, more sensitive detection technique of clusterization has been established. This work demonstrates the value of theoretical models in identifying key experimental challenges and demonstrating the feasibility of experimental implementations, a collaboration that is a cornerstone of any successful experimental and theoretical scientific endeavor. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit recurrence times for their outbursts that exceed a decade when observed from within the Galactic center; what's more, their observed minimum recurrence time is as long as 10 years, much greater than what's expected under established theoretical models. This challenge to the established theoretical framework of neutron star binaries' behavior may have implications for the search for intermediate mass black holes and the explanation of outbursts in some ultraluminous X-ray sources. Furthermore, because many of these long interval sources exhibit no outbursts in the 2-10 keV energy range but do in higher energies, their presence may be underestimated in current X-ray surveys. This idea is also put to test by the discovery of a new variable source toward the Sagittarius arm using a combination of X-ray data from the Chandra, XMM-Newton, and the Swift X-ray observatory, whose behavior during outbursts suggests it holds important information for determining whether a particular X-ray transient is actually an intermediate mass black hole candidate. Lastly, because the newly developed model of neutron star spin periods aligns with those of most X-ray transients, it challenges the notion that an X-ray transient's spin period is a suitable indicator of its black hole nature. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the distribution of neutron star binaries' recurrence times and their behavior during outbursts is essential for accurately identifying and validating the presence of intermediate mass black holes in the galaxy. This, in turn, will provide a more accurate view of galaxy evolution and the population of compact objects that have gone missing. This study thus highlights the need for continued X-ray monitoring of candidate X-ray transients across a broader energy range in order to fully comprehend the behavior of these sources and accurately determine the population of black holes in the galaxy. Additionally, a better understanding of the relationship between radio and X-ray binaries within the galaxy will be achieved through a wider energy range monitoring of candidate X-ray transients and a greater emphasis on searching for radio counterparts of X-ray binaries that exhibit no outbursts

Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity

This advanced system utilizes deep learning and temporal sequence analysis to recognize patterns of behavior from a dataset with annotated risk indicators, and was optimized using various feature extractors for maximum effectiveness, ultimately achieving a 0.937 AUC score. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. When comparing these scenarios to each other and to the theoretical limitations imposed by the law of gravity, we found that in most cases, the most limiting factor for a star's development was its potential for mass loss due shedding, rather than slow-down. This effect was particularly evident in models starting from normal mass ranges. However, in models beginning from lower mass ranges, a third scenario could occur, where the star spins so fast that its equator breaks and matter is shed due to this break-up, resulting in a narrower shape and further mass shedding. This 'bifurcation' effect wasn't visible in previous modeling due to its limitations. To model this break-up, the programming had to be modified to consider objects that aren't symmetrical. This change allowed modeling of objects spinning so fast that they experience this type of extreme breakdown. This new understanding of low-mass star formation challenges a previously held theory about the necessity of magnetic fields in low-mass star formation. It suggests that magnetic fields aren't necessary for low-mass stars and rather, this type of star formation can occur in environments without magnetic fields, as long as rotation rates are high enough. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. The comprehensive investigation conducted here paves the way for exploring additional techniques to counter scoring bias in the context of big, imbalanced datasets. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to the presence of surgical implants, respiratory and cardiac dysfunction, and varying age and disease type. Furthermore, there is a lack of available training data for rare congenital heart diseases, making it difficult to accurately diagnose TOF patients through this method. This research aims to investigate the effectiveness of using a specifically trained U-Net algorithm on a comprehensive CMR data set from adults with heart diseases, but then applying it to CMR images of TOF patients not included in the training data. If successful, this method could streamline the 3D analysis of heart images without the need for manual expert input. The results of this study show that, although the U-Net algorithm yielded high accuracy ratings on the training and validation sets, its application to CMR images of TOF patients not included in the training data yielded significantly inferior outcomes. In order to enhance its performance on unseen data, the time it took to achieve the initial high accuracy ratings on the validation set needed to be increased to at least five-fold the current number of training iterations. This outcome was anticipated due to the limited size and diversity of the data used for training the primary network. Furthermore, employing a data augmentation technique known as progressive residual density functional network resulted in a significant improvement in outcome, but it was difficult to determine if this improvement was solely the result of the added density functional layer. This research findings are significant, given that accurate image analysis is a crucial precursor to the surgical planning and monitoring of TOF patients undergoing pulmonary valve replacement, and thus further work is needed to validate and refine this method against a larger and more diverse data set of CMR images of TOF patients. The primary goal of this research project is to explore the feasibility of developing an accurate, automated and multi-user compatible analysis tool for use in the clinical management of these patients. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Our findings also reveal that distilling the knowledge from a CNN can be a viable approach to enhance the performance of shallow FPN levels. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yy3651126/dist-fpn. This research paves the way for a more profound understanding of neural networks and the integration of high-level context is also discussed. Furthermore, our analysis and methods can facilitate the incorporation of other complex neural networks within the detection framework. In particular, our results demonstrate that a simple CNN can outperform the current state-of-the-art detection models incorporating cumbersome Context-aware Bastions (CABs) modules that are utilized with a Context-aware Transformer (Kastner et al., 2022) module on the COCO benchmark. Our analysis and experiments provide a pathway for the design of next-generation detection models. Moreover, our study on the distribution of backpropagation paths can facilitate a deeper understanding of the backward passes in higher layer networks, such as transformer layers, which is also being investigated in related fields like training neural networks with random weights. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. The obtained distribution shows that the standard power-law model is inaccurate and should be replaced by a truncated version. Furthermore, the study finds that the location of the power-law exponent within the distribution provides valuable immunization information. In fact, the micro-level analysis of node removal sizes is shown to be more sensitive to network parameters than standard component-size methods. Consequently, this study demonstrates that attacking nodes located at the shortest path between the root and the leaves is the most effective strategy. Additionally, a comparative analysis with theoretical models confirms that the obtained distribution can be mapped back to the standard power-law model only when the attack probability is extremely low. Moreover, a discussion on potential extensions to general network structures is also presented. By applying the micro-level approach to network analysis, this study paves the way for a more precise understanding of network phenomena. Furthermore, this study's findings on node removal sizes in Cayley tree networks can be incorporated into epidemiological models that take into account the effects of individual node removals. Moreover, these models can be used to develop more targeted immunization strategies that address specific network vulnerabilities. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, the sloshing Sagnac design can be implemented using the existing infrastructure of advanced detectors with only minor modifications. Furthermore, the end mirrors can be placed at a non-equidistant position, and this degree of freedom offers scope for further optimization of the detector performance. The potential of this design to overcome the limitations of conventional detectors makes it an attractive option for the next generation of gravitational wave detectors. The improvement in sensitivity offered by this design could also be incorporated into conventional signal-recycled systems by increasing the degree of phase modulation, thus providing a practical path to achieving similar performance improvements. The challenges and complexities of the sloshing Sagnac design also highlight the benefits and scope for incorporating non-conventional architectures in quantum signal recovery problems, as demonstrated with the example of applying machine learning optimization techniques to outdo conventional homodyne probing strategies. The performance of this new design surpasses that of conventional systems, offering a 8% improvement in sensitivity at 400 Hz, a 25% improvement at 700 Hz, and a 173% improvement at 1000 Hz, or equivalently, a 6.5% increase in signal-to-noise ratio at 400 Hz, a 34% increase at 700 Hz, and a 201% increase at 1000 Hz for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms. The implementation of the sloshing Sagnac design could potentially overcome the limitations of conventional detectors and offer improved performance in the high-frequency range, or provide better detection capabilities for certain merger waveforms. The design could potentially be implemented with only minor modifications to the existing infrastructure of advanced detectors, and the performance of this new design surpasses that of conventional systems, offering a 8% improvement

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces data transfer delays, and significantly boosts overall connectivity. Furthermore, numerical simulations show that devices with larger reception areas tend to cause congestion, but the new protocol effectively manages this issue. Furthermore, when the number of devices increases dramatically, as expected in future applications, the new protocol's efficiency in managing interference and extending connectivity to all devices is assured. The new protocol's efficiency also makes it compatible with a wide range of MIMO applications. The reasons behind the improved performance of the new protocol are its ability to utilize under-laid visibility areas, reduce inter-device interference, and achieve better throughput per device. The new protocol achieves better performance than traditional protocols by allocating the same number of signal shares as other approaches but reassigns them to provide faster data transfer in devices with larger reception areas. The results obtained with this new protocol are validated through further simulations that examine the effects of varying system parameters such as the number of devices, reception areas, and signal shares. The outcomes of these simulations provide valuable insights into future MIMO applications design, particularly the importance of considering the variability of devices' reception areas. The new protocol introduces some delays in data transfer in devices with smaller reception areas but the reasons for this are the priority scheduling of devices with larger reception areas and the increased throughput per device achieved with faster data transfer. The results obtained with this new protocol are comparable to those achieved with alternative approaches that manage interference by scheduling devices with different reception areas but the new protocol delivers these performance levels with a much simpler design. The new protocol enables the achievement of high throughput transfer rates in crowded environments by providing fast data transfer in devices with larger reception areas and the necessary throughput in devices with smaller reception areas. The new protocol's ability to manage the variability of devices' reception areas has significant implications for future MIMO applications that will require the co-existence of devices

This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. Our findings indicate that balanced molmer-sorensen gates can withstand frequency fluctuations up to several megahertz, essentially offering a robust solution for quantum applications prone to frequency fluctuations, in contrast to conventional molmer-sorensen gates that are highly sensitive to frequency distortions. Furthermore, this method can easily incorporate multiple motional modes, making it particularly suitable for quantum simulations involving multi-peak entanglement, and further development of this gate design for use with other trapped particles, such as superconducting phase fluctuations, may also be feasible.

This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer. However, this interpretation holds true only in certain situations. We investigate and illustrate with examples that in other situations, the spectral shift around anomalies in the Sagnac interferometer may behave contrary to this understanding, thereby being characterized as spectral switch anomalies. We also examine the conditions under which a gyroscope's angular momentum and the Gyroscope-Rotating-Inside-a-Gyro (GRIG) system may exhibit this counterintuitive behavior. Moreover, we propose that in the GRIG setup, the gyroscope's angular momentum has a distinct effect on the spectral shift around anomalies, different from that of a gyroscope placed within it. Furthermore, we establish that the GRIG system may serve as a spectral switch anomaly generator for potential use in energy harvesting or demodulation applications. We conclude by highlighting the potential for the GRIG system to incorporate a class of nonlinear elements, such as nonlinear resonators, for further exploration. Additionally, we offer a general method for the GRIG system to produce multiple spectral switch anomalies within a narrower frequency range. This approach can also be applied to create a hybrid system that generates a spectral switch anomaly in both the near and mid-infrared regions. Lastly, we contemplate the possibility of developing a gyroscope-based spectral switch anomaly generator for potential use in demodulation applications. This concept may pave the way for further exploration in combining gyroscopes with nonlinear elements, such as nonlinear resonators, to harvest energy from a broad range of sources or to develop a new method for position location in high-speed applications. Furthermore, we propose that a gyroscope-based spectral switch anomaly generator may provide an advantage over conventional methods in applications involving the detection of moving objects or systems in motion. This could potentially enable the detection of objects or systems in motion even when the frequency of the moving object or system is higher than the detection bandwidth. This approach may also be more accurate and efficient than conventional methods in certain situations. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes. Our findings provide a pathway for the $n$-gram model to regain prominence in the face of competing neural models, primarily due to its balance of exceptional performance, meager computational requirements, and the flexibility it affords when adapting to new languages or domains. Furthermore, our approach offers a novel solution for the efficient training of neural models on vast datasets, allowing for the incorporation of the $n$-gram model as a form of data augmentation, reducing the necessity for extensive dataset training. Our results, coupled with the relatively compact model size (approximately 50 million parameters), suggest that our hybrid approach embodies the optimal blend of performance, efficiency, and flexibility, rendering it the ideal model for a broad spectrum of text-related applications. This study proposes a novel, unified framework for semantic parsing that enables text-to-SQL on multiple databases. This means a single training session can effectively prepare a parser to successfully translate texts into SQL code across various databases.
