This improvement stems from generating more diverse and comprehensive code, which in turn enables our model to efficiently handle ambiguities and unseen situations. Through experiments, our unified parser achieves nearly identical performance when tested against datasets collected from individual databases and also demonstrates robust performance in cross-domain evaluations, proving that it adeptly handles out-of-domain data. This research is significant because it's the first of its kind to present a full-fledged, cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing framework. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Furthermore, the mapping from loom spaces to veering triangulations is found to be one-to-one, with a base in Bielawski-Fenster-Zhang's symmetry. A method to create veering triangulations is established through the use of train tracks that maintain invariance under the action of loom space homeomorphisms' derivatives. A key component of this proof involves a graphic representation called a Loday graph, which serves as a combinatorial description of both loom spaces and train tracks with this property. A direct connection between Loday graphs and train tracks that satisfy the mentioned condition is established, along with a less direct connection that enables the generation of veering triangulations from their combinatorial descriptions. A associated train track, derived from this relationship, possesses specific combinatorial characteristics which result in a veering triangulation. A notable aspect of this result is the appearance of two distinct veering triangulations for a given loom space, arising from the action of reflecting homeomorphisms across leaves that are geodesic paths between two fixed points. This phenomenon's connection to Gu\'eritaud's research on loom spaces rooted in ribbon surface geometry is also explored. A further extension of train tracks that satisfy the mentioned condition is a set of crosscutting systems for all surfaces of a specified type, with a related Loday graph displaying a particular symmetry. This property enables the creation of veering triangulations for a broader class of surfaces, contributing to a better comprehension of Gu\'eritaud's research. A final section is dedicated to a broader discussion and potential future directions in the field. A comprehensive appendix is included, addressing additional technical details and a key component in the research, the application of the Poincar\'e-Hopf Theorem. A further clarification is provided for the relationship between loom spaces, train tracks, and Loday graphs through the use of a key property called "QC". A cross-reference between the notation used in the paper's main sections and the expanded definitions in the appendix is also included. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. A significant reduction of over 90% of edges in the PubMed dataset is also attainable with Kedge using a softer sparsification method, paving the way for more complex graph edge sparsification techniques that can be applied to a broad range of GNN models. The code for Kedge is publicly available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/Kedge. The technique's efficacy is backed by thorough theoretical justifications and rigorous experiments, showcasing its potential as a groundbreaking approach for the interpretable use of GNNs in critical domains. The implementation of Kedge within a full pipeline is detailed in our upcoming workshop paper at the 2022 NeurIPS Workshop on Interpretable Neural Progrmming, available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.01751. The recent study in arXiv paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02098 using Kedge along with the comprehensive analysis of the latter's arXiv article https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.01508 further validate the technique's effectiveness. The issue of graph edge sparsification was initially explored in our earlier conference paper at ICLR'21 at https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.04281, and our later investigation in the NIPS'21 workshop paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.01751, leading to the complete implementation and rigorous evaluation presented here. The current study provides a thorough mathematical framework for the technique in question in the 2022 EMLA

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Interestingly, this outcome is almost optimal, given that a k times improvement is achievable without any increase in query count. Furthermore, a new, albeit less efficient, method was presented that, although involving more queries, achieves a similar level of robustness to at least logarithmic sketch sizes, a development that could have broader implications. The concept of strong foolering was defined, offering a new framework for analyzing the robustness of sketches, and this framework was utilized to demonstrate that the classic estimator for axis-oriented sketches exhibits a k times decline in effectiveness, regardless of sketch size, and that a simple modification to foole-resistant sketches results in sketches that, although less efficient, remain robust. A new estimator was proposed, based on a multi-linear sketch, which, although less efficient and offering lower accuracy for specific components, always retains some level of effectiveness, a property that holds true for any feedback scenario. The challenges and limitations of this approach are also discussed in the context of current techniques for designing robust dimensionality reduction methods. The potential of a combination of foole-resistant sketches and unique estimators, tailored to particular situations, to achieve optimal results is also touched upon. Furthermore, the potential of a multi-linear sketch that can handle any level of feedback, based on a specific combination of feedsom sketches, is also discussed. The paper is concluded by outlining the potential of further research into the strong foolering concept and new estimator frameworks for a broader range of dimensionality reduction applications. The results of this study, particularly the development of a k times improved estimator for CountSketch sketches and a new, albeit less efficient, method, offer a significant contribution to our understanding of the robustness of dimensionality reduction methods, providing a k times improvement factor that is nearly optimal and a new, albeit less efficient, method that could have broader implications for the field. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This new formalism develops a set of conservation principles, including the conservation of angular momentum, to create a simplified and consistent framework for predicting the outcomes of these complex processes. This model distinguishes the various types of multiple star systems based on their geometric configurations, such as collinear, V shaped, and equilateral triples, to create a comprehensive framework for predicting the outcomes of these processes. This model also identifies key parameters that determine the behavior of these systems, such as the mass ratio in binary systems and the mass ratio and orbital period in higher order multiples. This research will significantly expand our understanding of the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This new approach to predicting the outcomes of these complex processes will significantly expand our understanding of these processes, and will likely result in a major revision of our current understanding of the behavior of these binary and multiple star systems. This new formalism will be tested against all of the available observational constraints, such as the distribution of post common envelope binaries, the distribution of the masses of the white dwarfs, as well as the rates of all types of compact object mergers and supernovae

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. 

Despite being highly compact and rotating rapidly, the galaxy at the center of our study exhibits outflow properties similar to those of more slowly rotating galaxies, suggesting that rotation rate is not a primary factor in outflow strength. In addition to enhancing outflow mass, a recently formed young stellar population also plays a crucial role in outflow power, while the global outflow mass is primarily governed by outflow speed. Our study further reveals that high-power outflows can lead to gas being ejected from the galaxy, contributing to the overall cosmic matter cycle. 

Observations of this galaxy provide a critical testing ground for models of outflow formation, offering insights into the relationship between outflows and other galaxy properties, such as rotation, gas composition, and the formation of supermassive black holes. Given the limitations of current telescopes, a combination of upgraded facilities like CCFS/CCROWD and the use of submm-wavelength telescopes will be necessary to study outflows in higher-z galaxies. 

Our study with multiple facilities on Mauna Kea, including KCWI, NOEMA, and HST, highlights the value of a holistic approach to studying galaxy formation and the critical role of outflows in converting gas into stars, a process also regulated by other factors such as gas composition and the formation of supermassive black holes. 

The data presented in this paper will be useful to researchers studying the complex relationships between outflows, star formation rates, and gas composition in galaxies, as well as the limitations of outflow mass when converting gas into stars, and the need for future high-resolution, high-z outflow studies with upgraded facilities like CCFS/CCROWD.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  Compared to leading Big Data processing technologies, Spark has been found to offer the best balance of scalability, performance, and ease of integration, resulting in which DistQualityAssessment can handle very large datasets of up to 32 gigabytes with ease, achieving notable speed gains over traditional single-machine implementations.  With the continuous growth of Linked Data, our distributed framework is critical in addressing upcoming challenges related to data quality, thereby creating new opportunities and potential for further innovation and advancement. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating the parameters of a stochastic process that underlies the data, based on the minimum density power divergence estimator. This results in a well-defined maximum likelihood type estimate even in the absence of a specified model, and its properties are analyzed leading to $\sqrt{n}$ consistency and an asymptotic distribution under mild conditions. As the method is computationally efficient and simple to implement, especially in comparison to other alternatives, it is deemed a viable solution for large-scale data sets. The paper also facilitates access to R software for its implementation. Despite the method's effectiveness, it is essential to acknowledge that under ideal conditions, the maximum likelihood estimator remains the most effective option. The paper's approach is particularly well-suited for modeling time series data, and it discusses the challenges and limitations of applying the method to subseries data. The paper also explores the consequences of conditioning on the data when evaluating the properties of the estimator, and it identifies specific conditions under which the normal approximation can be applied with confidence intervals. The paper's findings are verified through simulations, and it also provides a context in which the standard maximum likelihood estimator continues to perform better than the robust estimator. The paper is also a discussion of my PhD research. The standard maximum likelihood estimator is highly efficient when working with data generated by a specified model; however, it lacks resilience to anomalies in the data, which can significantly impact forecasts. As forecasts often aim to predict rare and extreme events, and as the robust estimator's performance decreases in such instances, the paper raises the question of whether the improvement in estimates' reliability is worth the decrease in efficiency. This issue is further complicated by the fact that in some contexts, the standard estimator performs better than the robust estimator. This problem is particularly pronounced in weather forecasting, as the aim is to predict rare and extreme weather events. As the paper's research is related to but distinct from forecasting, it is not clear whether the results have any implications for this field. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Our approach achieved a 47% gain in distance-aware benchmark evaluations and we believe our work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of this challenge and more effective approaches to solving it. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Our findings provide a basis for identifying whether a non-bipartite cubic graph is perfect-matching-Hamiltonian by comparing its structure to that of the papillon graphs. The last section of our research involves a related theorem related to edge-colourings. A cubic graph's edge-colouring is Hamiltonian if and only if its dual graph also has a Hamiltonian path. This dual relationship may provide a basis for determining whether a cubic graph has a Hamiltonian path. A related theorem is also presented about the relationship between cubic graphs and their duals concerning 2-factors. A vast family of 3-edge-colourable graphs, described as papillon-like, are also introduced and their properties regarding the PMH-property and E2F condition explored. Our work lays the groundwork for future investigation into the properties of these new families and whether their members with the PMH-property always satisfy the E2F condition. The challenges of applying deep reinforcement learning in complex, dynamic systems like soccer are significant, but our success paves the way for subsequent research to build upon our findings and the proposed approach. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for a potential improvement in image quality. The concept of time-domain extended sources is introduced as a simple physical interpretation of time-dependent sources that can be achieved using a non-zero source duration. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in simulated data scenarios.  Additionally, a discussion on the implications of non-zero source duration in the data and the generated wavefields is presented, and it is concluded that time-domain extended sources can be modeled as a combination of Ricker wavelets with the same central frequency as the data, without compromising the accuracy of the formulations.  Furthermore, numerical results using real data demonstrate the potential of time-domain extended sources to produce more detailed images than the classical FWI.  Finally, the potential of time-domain extended sources to produce multiple image realizations from a single shot dataset is also discussed.  The formulations can be modified to incorporate additional physical constraints, such as source and receiver limitations, and the use of real data recorded with extended sources. The extensions of time-domain extended sources to 3D and time-domain extended sources with time-dependent source spectrum are also discussed. electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. Additionally, we introduce a publicly accessible, more
robust version of the SCAPE dataset, encompassing the annotations of 11
scholarly studies on semantic change. This enhanced dataset is applicable to
all methods employed in our study. Furthermore, we introduce the SCS task
at the COLING 2020 conference, where our ensemble method ranked second but
failed to meet the stringent requirements set by the task organizers due to
its limited use of contextualized information. We explore various contextualized
language models to gain insight into their performances, along with their
underlying characteristics. Lastly, we explore two alternative methods for
capturing difficult cases and propose the application of two distinct word
representation techniques. One method combines the results of different
contextualized models, while the other employs a character-based model as a
supplementary source of information. This approach yields an enhanced
ensemble method with the highest overall accuracy of 73.19%. The outcomes of
our study suggest that although contextualized language models excel in
many domains, they may not be the most suitable choice for analyzing
diachronic semantic changes. More notably, our results indicate that words
with significant contextual fluctuations, fluctuating meanings, or no change
pose a persistent challenge to any method employed. Furthermore, our study
identifies crucial aspects to be considered in the design of future word
representation models, including the difficulty of words, their grammatical
component, and the complexity of their contextual fluctuations. Ultimately,
our study underscores the importance of employing a more comprehensive
approach

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of quasar spins into ultralight scalar, vector, or tensor properties results in the formation of a broad distribution of possible values. Nonetheless, certain restrictions on the properties of these ultralight bosons can be imposed based on the characteristics of heavy quasars, specifically their spin. The analysis of the properties of these ultralight bosons is approached from two angles: the first method utilizes the minimum possible spin of heavy quasars to determine the ultralight boson mass, while the second method leverages the maximum spin to derive the ultralight boson mass. The resulting mass ranges for the ultralight bosons are tightly constrained, with the scalar mass falling within the range (1.3~$\rm \times~10^{-20}$ eV to 2.3~$\rm \times~10^{-21}$ eV), the vector mass within the range (4.4~$\rm \times~10^{-23}$ eV to 7.9~$\rm \times~10^{-23}$ eV), and the tensor mass within the range (2.5~$\rm \times~10^{-22}$ eV to 4.5~$\rm \times~10^{-22}$ eV). These findings provide a basis for investigating the interactions between ultralight bosons and dark matter, as well as ultralight boson compositeness, in the context of heavy quasars. The behavior of these ultralight bosons may also give rise to observable signatures in the electromagnetic spectra of AGNs. The strategy outlined in this research can be applied to the study of a broader range of phenomena involving ultralight bosons. The properties of these ultralight bosons are critically dependent on spin constraints for heavy quasars, underscoring the significance of accurately determining quasar spin. The results presented in this study highlight the value of further investigations into quasar spin and the properties of ultralight bosons, as well as the potential for new discoveries in the study of heavy quasars. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, our findings are applicable to other
tissues exhibiting IKNM, such as the developing telencephalon and spinal cord in zebrafish. Our research demonstrates
that the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM can be understood through simple physical principles, likely uncovering a
universal underlying mechanism common to all systems characterized by IKNM. By further exploring the relationship
between cell fate choice and position within these systems, our findings may reveal the underlying mechanisms governing
the random selection of cell fate. Our study also demonstrates that, at least in the zebrafish retina, cell fate choice is
randomly selected in a specific, stratified environment, where each layer has unique gene expression profiles. Moreover,
our research enables the creation of a computational model that can simulate the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM,
enabling the generation of realistic migration tracks and accurate maps of densely packed nuclei across the retina. This
model can be employed to investigate how alterations in the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper surface, nuclear
movement, and cell fate choice impact the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. By exploring these factors, our study may
shed light on the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM in other systems. Our study
also provides a framework for uncovering the mechanisms governing the random selection of cell fate within these systems. 
Our results demonstrate that in zebrafish retinas, cell fate choice is randomly selected in a specific, stratified environment

Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
Additionally, we outline that the exceptional van Hove singularity 
can also emerge in other pseudogap metals, such as fergusonite metals, 
and that our general framework can be applied across these contexts. 
Furthermore, we explore the potential for the exceptional van Hove singularity 
to provide a broader theoretical framework that can be expanded upon in future 
developments, and that the proposed metallic state can be experimentally 
identified through direct observation of the merged Fermion segments. 
Finally, we suggest that the exceptional van Hove singularity may hold the key 
to a more comprehensive understanding of the diverse, material-dependent 
pseudogap states that may exist within the broader family of cuprate materials. 
In the case of YBCO, we propose that the exceptional van Hove singularity 
arises due to an unusual electronic structure resulting from a specific 
orientational relationship between adjacent CuO$_2$ layers, 
and that this leads to a distinct, pseudogap-induced orbital order, 
which may also give rise to the experimental observed of spiral correlations. 
The proposed theory also provides a new perspective on the electronic structure 
of optimal-doped YBCO, suggesting that the typical description of this material 
as a Luttinger fluid may not be entirely accurate, 
and that a more precise, band-structure description may be attainable. 
The concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity is then further applied 
to explain the experimental data of optimal-doped BSCCO, 
and it is demonstrated that this may also give rise to a Lifshitz 
transition, however, in this case, the electronic structure is believed to 
be driven by a stronger electronic interaction

The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. The data this apparatus collects will also contribute to research involving cosmic-neutron background spectra in underground locations. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The TKS dataset is available at the Exoplanet Open Data Table and the target selection code is available at the Exoplanet Software Catalog. The TESS-Keck Survey highlights the significance of combining transit and radial velocity observations in tandem, a methodology that it hopes will be incorporated into future mission guidelines and resource allocations. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, they highlight the importance of further investigating the continuum of human object knowledge and the potential disparities between human and machine vision. Moreover, our study provides insight into the localized neural mechanisms behind human agency perception in animals, a process thought to involve multiple systems when confronted with human social interactions. This research lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive reappraisal of the animacy spectrum in VTC and suggests that similar continua may exist across other domains of human object knowledge. Additionally, our study implies that the overlap often observed between animal-sensitive regions may, in fact, result from the broader societal appreciation of animals that has driven human evolutionary history. This perspective is further supported by the agency perception networks that have developed in response to the unique human experience with animals, a perspective that may be applicable to other domains of human object knowledge that have been shaped by similar evolutionary forces. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. The modified logic retains the original's soundness proof and verification theorem, and we have demonstrated its utility by reproducing the proof of the quantum mean-payoff algorithm and deriving a reachability theorem suitable for cost-capsule programs. Additionally, we have investigated the limitations of the modified logic and proposed potential future extensions. The development of this modified logic is also soon to be presented as a tutorial at the Quantitative Program Analysis Workshop 2022. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Nonetheless, some issues with our network remain unresolved, and future research aims to tackle them through strategies such as data augmentation and non-cumulative training methods. Despite these limitations, our study demonstrates the feasibility of resolving the sign problem using artificial neural networks. Furthermore, we verify that our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art schemes, including the exponential neural network and the Hubert sign problem cancellation scheme, as evidenced by our numerical results for the 2D Hubbard model. Our findings suggest that our method surpasses the efficiency of these competitors in terms of energy minimization cost. Additionally, we observe a significant improvement in the accuracy of our results, confirming the potential of complex-valued neural networks to effectively tackle the sign problem. Our implementation of this architecture in the Monte Carlo framework is made available through an open-source Python package called mc-nn, accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/awadhwa/mc-nn. Furthermore, our results for the 2D Hubbard model with 32 electrons are presented in the accompanying figure, displaying an energy reduction of approximately three orders of magnitude achieved in 20 minutes using 6 GPUs. This groundbreaking achievement brings us closer to resolving the sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations for systems that were previously unexplored. As a result, a much larger subset of lattice models can now be investigated with high precision. This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand had initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true. 

As for Pomerance, he had a more specific question regarding the count of y-friable powers of prime numbers in the range from 1 to x, which we also address by providing a new formula that gives the count of y-friable powers of prime numbers for $y$ in the range from $(1+\varepsilon)\log x$ to $\log x$. This new formula reveals that once $y$ reaches $\alpha\log x$ with $1.516\ge \alpha > 1$, the count of y-friable powers of prime numbers would be less than 1 and for any given prime number $p$, there will be a value of $x$ large enough such that the count of y-friable powers of prime number $p$ in the range from 1 to x will be less than 1 when $y$ is smaller than $\alpha\log x$. 

We also discuss alternative ways to express the count of y-friable integers by estimating the count of y-friable powers of prime numbers.

The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. This comprehensive database of planetary nebulae is now available for further scientific investigations of the dynamics and star formation history within galaxies. Furthermore, by incorporating spatially resolved measurements of the mass of the dark matter within galaxies, a fundamental constant used in the calculation was validated through independent distance measurements to Fornax cluster galaxies. A single universal value of 3.8 was determined and compared to alternative methods, demonstrating its accuracy. This research is also accompanied by an educational guide on the analysis procedures used, including step-by-step instructions and a comprehensive list of the theoretical and observational assumptions made throughout the study. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We demonstrate this sensitivity applies to multiple neural network architectures, across diverse datasets, and with various regularization techniques, ultimately showing there is no single, universally superior loss function. In response to these discoveries, we propose a novel, adaptive loss function framework capable of autonomously identifying the most effective loss function for a given problem, leading to performance enhancements of up to 12% across different datasets. The proposed framework's benefits are showcased through an interactive visualization tool, making it easy to experience the complex performance dynamics underlying deep learning classification in relation to loss function variation. In conclusion, our research highlights the importance of viewing loss function choice as a parameter with far-reaching implications for the performance of deep learning classification, giving rise to a new direction in the pursuit of optimized, adaptive solutions. The intricate performance landscape resulting from loss function variation is a fundamental aspect of deep learning that necessitates a more flexible, adaptable loss function design, capable of emerging optimal performance from the diverse range of loss functions available. This goal is now within reach, thanks to the introduction of a cutting-edge, neuroevolutionary loss function framework that provides a viable solution. This research provides a significant milestone in the evolution of deep learning, marking a major departure from fixed loss function approaches that will be influential in guiding the evolution of future deep learning technologies. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. Our results demonstrate improvement over not normalizing the feedback and also show that reward feedback, although unexpected, can still be utilized to the agent's advantage. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  ATOMIC is made up of seven sub-datasets that are diverse in terms of the types of conditional relationships they contain.  Three of these sub-datasets were utilized in conjunction with publicly accessible text datasets, while the other four sub-datasets were constructed using a web-based crowdsourcing platform.  The design of these sub-datasets showcases various aspects of human inference, such such as the consequences of performing actions and the outcomes of certain events, along with the evaluation of other individuals, the initiation of actions, and the consequences of emotional states.  To provide a comprehensive evaluation of his dataset, our team designed multiple text-based classification tasks that are relevant to the conditional relationships and diverse in terms of their underlying structure.  This was coupled with a pioneering approach that incorporates unstructured descriptions of relational facts into learning algorithms.  Our experiments revealed that machine learning models that are trained on ATOMIC but lack any explicit relation structure, still exhibit a capacity for learning relation structures from examples, when compared to baselines and other available datasets.  Moreover, our findings demonstrate that through additional training on instances of these relations, these models are capable of extending the knowledge in ATOMIC to a wide range of scenario-based four-part connections (X causes Y in Z).  This includes numerous human emotions and the initiation of actions which are unique components of conditional relationships and distinct from other available datasets that are centered on categorization.  This means that machine learning models that are trained on ATOMIC are better equipped to handle a broader range of everyday scenario-based inferential tasks.  This is supported by results showing that these models are more accurate in tasks that are structured around four-part connections (X causes Y in Z) than those operating in isolation.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The conditions $k_n$ is much smaller than $n$ also enables us to derive non-asymptotic bounds. The techniques developed in this paper can be applied more broadly to other conditionally symmetric random walk settings. This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space. The algorithm is an adaptation of the method proposed by E. B. Elliott to yield polyhedra with non-cubic bases. The Elliott method is a recursive approach to constructing fully transitive polyhedra, starting from the unit cube in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. The Elliott method involves two primary steps: the splitting step and the merging step. The splitting step divides a given polyhedron into two distinct components, whereas the merging step combines two component polyhedra. However, both of these steps are only guaranteed to produce a combined polyhedron with a transitive action when the original polyhedra are themselves equipped with fully transitive actions. The Elliott method therefore necessitates the use of a secondary procedure, known as the Elliott process, to validate the combined polyhedron's action. The Elliott process is an inductive process that relies on a key dimensionality invariant known as the Elliott invariant. The algorithm devised by Eisenlohr and Farris simplifies the Elliott method by directly addressing the merging step's guarantee, effectively eliminating the need for the Elliott process. As such, this algorithm enables the generation of fully transitive polyhedra through a straightforward, recursive approach. Furthermore, this algorithm facilitates the integration of distinct component polyhedra via the merging step, thereby providing a versatile framework for a wide range of applications. The paper's authors' interests lie in its relevance to Euclidean geometry, geometry-based coding, and three-dimensional vision. The algorithm's versatility, however, suggests its potential utility in various other contexts. The algorithm's implementation is made available to the community via an affiliated repository. The algorithm's performance is examined in a limited capacity, and several novel polyhedra are presented in the paper's appendix. The paper's final section outlines several directions for further exploration or enhancement of the algorithm. The algorithm's name is a combination of the names J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, and we provide an alternative analysis, alongside a cloning attack on their scheme that surpasses the previously known success rate. This improvement, however, comes at the cost of reducing the overall security from negligible advantage to one that is quadratic in the number of ciphertexts.

  - New Applications: We've discovered connections between unclonable encryption and other cryptographic concepts, including unforgeable encryption, public-key encryption with designation, and non-committal encryption. We've established constructions for both public-key and private-key settings, and we discuss potential future directions for unclonable encryption within the context of these related fields. Additionally, we've introduced a new unclonable encryption goal centered on designing constructions where the original message can be recovered upon presentation of two encrypted versions, and we explored its implications in the context of both public-key and private-key settings.... Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. It highlights the potential for further research
enabled by a better understanding of the analogous processes in these diverse
objects, as well as the likelihood that studying both stars and planets will yield
new discoveries. It also emphasizes the value of utilizing existing data more
effectively and the importance of future observations that can reveal key details
about their physical properties. This will involve a high level of coordination
among different observational and theoretical studies of both stars and planets. 
It is essential to recognize that both entities exhibit unique features, such as the
variability properties of the rapidly rotating small star PI Cetus and the radio
ocean on the super-Earth K2-18 b, which hold the key to understanding their
evolutionary histories and potential for supporting life. This review is an
outcome of the workshop "Winds and Magnetospheres of Stars and Planets: Similarities
and Differences" held at the MPIfA in Göttingen, Germany, from the 18th to 20th of
April 2018. It is being published in a special issue of the Astronomy & Astrophysics
journal. This review is a collaborative effort of the participants at the

In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models. 
The issue of whether neural networks can learn the complex agreement patterns
found in Basque languages serves as the primary focus of our study.
We base our agreement prediction task on two exercises: one in which the
models are given the entire sentence to inform their predictions and another
in which they are limited to analyzing just the sentence's prefix.
The outcomes of these experiments served as the foundation for our proposal
of a novel method called the Gap Measure.
The Gap Measure offers a straightforward statistical approach for evaluating
the performance difference between models' capabilities when they are given full
sentences versus just sentence prefixes.
The understanding of agreement prediction learned by neural networks is not
the same as that of the human eye, which is evident from additional
analyses carried out in conjunction with our findings.
As a consequence of our studies, we believe that future research should
examine neural network code using methods that emphasize the system's local
properties rather than its overall performance. 
On top of that, more attention should be paid to the way data is structured,
as well as the development of novel diagnostic tools that can compare the
understanding of sentence structures learned by different neural network
models. 
The recently released Basque Treebank also provides a solid foundation for

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Additionally, we investigate the potential of specialized processes, such as tau pair production with a spin correlation and the production of tau and neutrino pairs, to provide additional constraints on the properties of vector leptoquarks. These processes are also relevant to future experiments at future colliders, such as those involving electrons and protons at high energies.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. With potential applications in creating practical, lower-dose PET protocols, the code is also openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/krishna-ml/PET-resample. Furthermore, an interactive user interface called PET-Resample UI, also openly available at https://krishna-ml.github.io/PET-resample-UI/, enables researchers and clinicians to easily explore and apply this method to various scenarios. Limits and potential for future improvement of this model are also discussed in the findings. Experimental results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art models in multiple evaluation metrics. Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions. This article discusses the advantages and potential of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology in supervising the performance of network-based services. P2P's decentralized nature and capacity for flexible, self-adjusting networks make it suitable for developing more effective and automated methods of detecting performance standards violations. A basic design for a decentralized detection system, along with possible ways to implement it using P2P technologies, are also presented. Furthermore, future research directions in this area are outlined. To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards. The measurement obtained exceeded the minimum requirement of 0.5 barn by a significant margin, thus demonstrating the detector's capability to accurately measure neutron interactions across the desired energy range required for long-baseline neutrino experiments. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The developed framework facilitates the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings, complex motion planning, and learns from multiple demonstrations, surpassing individual expert performance. The EKMP code is publicly available at https://github.com/ethz-assistants/ekmp. For simple motion planning, we introduce a variant called Single Kernelized Movement Primitives (SKMP), which emulates the behavior of state-of-the-art motion planners, and includes a planning module that jointly considers all constraints. This paper was presented at the 2023 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). For complex skill learning, we introduce a related algorithm called Hierarchical Kernelized Movement Primitives (HKMP), that showcases a significant boost in learning capabilities. This hierarchical approach learns high-level obstacle avoidance strategies and decouples them from low-level motion planning, extending the capabilities of EKMP to a higher dimensionality expertise. This paper introduces a new evaluation metric for motion planning algorithms, and provides evaluations of our hierarchical framework through the solution of complex puzzle worlds, demonstrating its superiority over other methods. This paper was presented at the 2023 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). The code for the paper is publicly available at https://github.com/ethz-assistants/hkmp. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. This 45-degree rotation state, located very close to the point where the superconducting state is lost and characterized by a specific relationship between the sound wave's frequency and its resistance, may offer a more suitable starting point for the investigation of another, more distant transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure. This second transition is hypothesized to involve a more complex transformation of the square lattice structure into a triangular lattice and has significant implications for the understanding of the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism in these materials. However, further study is needed to confirm this second transition and the associated lattice structure change. This new evidence and the resulting understanding of the interlocked vortex lattice structure of these materials may have relevant implications for the broader scientific community. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. This metric shows that certain of our action sequence solutions precede dominant improvement points (DDPs) and, interestingly, that finding DDPs is equivalent to achieving optimal social welfare when action costs are positive. We observe that our proposed approach offers action sequences with nearly optimal social welfare when action costs are low. We experimentally validate our findings with extensive simulations and actual data, observing that our methods are generally capable of identifying action sequences with significant improvement over random serial dictatorship. We offer new and interesting theoretical results on the properties of combinatorial optimization problems when solved via action sequences and propose the challenging problem of designing efficient algorithms for solving optimization challenges with multiple agents in a serial dictatorship framework. We provide new and open questions for further investigation and present our code publicly available on GitHub. We also introduce a new machine learning model called the action sequence network, offering a novel way of modeling multiple agent action sequences. We experimentally assess the performance of this model, observing that it is capable of learning action sequences efficiently and provides a new way of solving optimization challenges through reinforcement learning. The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in the eastern and southwest parts of the basin with 2D methods yielded various velocity components for different geographic areas.  These velocity components were combined with block models to illustrate the separation process in the South Atlantic rift system.  The results show that initially slow extensional stretching led to a transition into sympassive and finally break-up phases.  The distinct timing of these phases varied across different regions of the basin.  The Runcorn-Peat (1966) model was supported, indicating that continental break-up occurred at different speeds in different parts of the basin.  The data suggest that the Amazon and Congo basins experienced continental break-up around 126 million years ago, whereas the Walvis and South Atlantic basins reached this stage about 125 and 126.5 million years ago respectively.  The results also indicate that the Amazon basin began experiencing extensional stretching at a time (126.5 million years ago) prior to the other regions of the South Atlantic.  The outcome of this research can be applied to the exploration for hydrocarbon reserves in the South Atlantic basin.  The study's findings on the history of the South Atlantic's rift system may also be relevant to other break-up events that occurred within the Gondwana supercontinent.  The results obtained from this research provide evidence that continental break-up in the South Atlantic occurred in an asymmetrical manner, a fact that has implications for the region's subsequent passive margin evolution.
