A trailblazing strategy was introduced in a prior study that successfully integrated information maximization with contrastive learning for self-supervised medical image segmentation. This approach involved treating image segmentation as a contrastive learning task that distinguishes a reconstructed image from the original, with the goal of optimizing a contrastive loss that maximizes the difference between them. A key aspect of this method involves extracting distinctive features from the image representations obtained through a learned encoder. To further enhance the quality of the encoder, this study introduced a novel boundary-aware information maximization (BI-MAX) framework that leverages the knowledge that medical image segmentations are notably crisp and well-defined. BI-MAX encodes the knowledge that valuable information resides within these distinct boundaries, allowing the development of an efficient encoder that extracts a wide range of informative features. The proposed framework demonstrates a notable increase in performance, achieving results that are just 85.3% of the original segmentation accuracy, thereby validating the effectiveness of BI-MAX. Moreover, the proposed framework exhibits versatility, with results indicating that it can adapt to various settings and produce consistent results, with mean intersection over union (IoU) scores ranging from 0.854 to 0.873. The source code of the proposed framework has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenDongDongDI/BIO16-Net. Furthermore, the study includes extensive empirical analyses and qualitative evaluations of the proposed framework, with results demonstrating its superiority over the baseline methods. The study also explores the integration of adversarial training with the proposed BI-MAX framework, with results indicating that it is possible to achieve even better performance with an encoder that is trained in an adversarial manner, with a mean IoU score of 0.894 achieved on the test dataset. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. This is particularly evident when the players' understanding is probed indirectly through their actions within that world. This approach holds significant value as it paves the way for the development of a wide range of collaborative applications that are both safe and engaging for all participants. These applications could be both text and voice-based, utilizing elements from role-playing games, such as characters with defined roles and responsibilities, to foster crucial life skills like empathy, navigation of complex social situations, and resilience in the face of challenging situations. Moreover, this type of training places the focus on the guiding aspect of human interaction rather than mere conversation, providing a model that easily adapts to new situations and settings, which is essential for creating both realistic and controllable interactive scenarios. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. When confronted with novel perturbation types, this approach allows for cost-effective counterfactual data generation, indicating that DISCO is an effective means of producing resilient models that are also versatile. The code for this study has been made publicly accessible on GitHub. As the field of counterfactual learning within NLP continues to evolve, we believe that DISCO's scalable, automated counterfactual data generation methodology will serve as a crucial benchmark. The technique's efficacy is demonstrated across not just text-based datasets but also datasets comprising only images of text, as shown in accompanying supplementary materials. These findings suggest that DISCO's broad applicability could usefully inform the development of future counterfactual learning methodologies. The scalar version of this framework has also been found to successfully generate high-quality counterfactual data for additional tasks, as revealed in the study's accompanying supplementary materials. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. As a result, our system excels in efficient learning for temporal sequences. Compared to conventional techniques, incorporating simultaneous supervised learning and metric adaptation enhances prediction accuracy in both synthetic and real-life scenarios, according to our results. Furthermore, the features identified by relevance learning show impressive comparisons to those of alternative methods. Additionally, our method allows for the visualization of low-dimensional grid data, highlighting the temporal structure in the data. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r.
Furthermore, we utilize this information to derive the optimal value for the sequence
reconstruction problem with a distance of d = 5 and r = 4, or with a distance of d = 2r
and r = 4; this value is achieved when there are at least 134 (respectively, 106) code
transmission channels used.
In contrast, we propose a code with a specific structure that achieves the same distance
of d = 5 with only 133 code transmission channels used when r = 4, or with a distance
of d = 2r and only 105 code transmission channels used.
This code construction leverages the properties of a Franklin code and includes a
specific permutation, in addition to obtaining the maximum possible overlap between
two spheres in a metric with a radius r = 4.
We anticipate that this code will be of use in other areas, such as cryptography. 
In particular cases where d = 2 or 3, we are able to provide bounds for the sequence
reconstruction problem; these bounds range from 2+2^r for a distance of d = 2 to 3+2^r-1
for a distance of d = 3.

real-world applications, and our research provides novel contributions to this area.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through both synthetic and real-world experiments involving audio features. The code for this project has been made available on the GitHub platform. The outcomes indicate that incorporating a hierarchical structure can enhance the accuracy of musical instrument detection in a few-shot learning setting. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. This initial exploration into this Question Answering subset, coupled with preliminary experiments on two subtasks, has laid the groundwork for future examinations of what Question Answering tools need to successfully navigate complex research papers in search of hidden information. The proposed QASPER dataset, comprising nearly 6,000 question-answer pairs over 1,585 NLP research papers, serves as a benchmark for evaluating the efficacy of these models, with the accompanying experiments highlighting substantial gaps between human and state-of-the-art model performance. This revised architecture, although quite basic, still lags behind human capabilities, as evidenced by the results presented herein. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. This analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of a Majorana fermion's status as both a particle and antiparticle. Finally, we demonstrate that the average energy of the Majorana ensemble is independent of the linear external potential, a unique finding that offers a novel method for determining the particle's mass. Additionally, we observe that the Majorana fermion's thermodynamic behavior is comparable to that of a Dirac fermion, although its statistical properties are distinct. Furthermore, we find that the Shannon entropy of the Majorana fermion is linked to its energy distribution, and both exhibit a similar dependence on the particle's mass. This relationship raises interesting questions about the particle's entropy in scenarios where its mass is not a fixed constant. Lastly, we explore the analogy between a Majorana fermion and a particle in a time-dependent, linear external potential, and identify an equivalent scenario involving a harmonic oscillator in a time-dependent potential. This equivalence has implications for our understanding of a Majorana fermion's behavior in electromagnetic fields. This complex interplay between the Majorana fermion's mass terms and its behavior in an external linear potential raises fundamental questions about the particle's status as both a particle and antiparticle. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. This dataset complements the existing Acronym Ontology, a comprehensive collection of defined acronyms first introduced in 2009, now enriched with 50 newly annotated documents. Acronyms identified within these documents are stored in a searchable database accessible via the system's homepage, showcasing its practical applications. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Finally, it contemplates the potential of artificial materials to surpass the limitations of their natural counterparts in the pursuit of a deeper understanding of topological physics. Feedback from practitioners and theorists within the field is actively solicited. This includes experts in topological insulators, condensed matter physics, photonics, and theoretical physics. In addition, individuals with expertise in optical communications and telecommunications are also highly encouraged to contribute their insights. This review is an open communication seeking input from the community to address the current knowledge on topological nodal lines. It aims to facilitate a discussion between researchers from these disciplines on the knowledge presented. This discussion will be continued through the presentation of the review at the 2019 Topological Insulation and Topological Nonzero-Pressure Nonlocal Transport Conference. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our methodology is applied to the recovery of textured non-Lambertian objects, and we showcase its efficacy in challenging cases involving diffuse illumination, shallow scenes, and plastic objects with varying rigidity and pose. Our approach achieves substantial improvement over baseline image-based optimization and failsafe descent methods, demonstrating the greatest accuracy across all tested scenarios. Furthermore, we find that our pre-trained model exhibits robust performance when adapted to novel datasets, outperforming the current state-of-the-art learning-based approach while requiring a significantly smaller parameter count. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. The accuracy of machine learning (ML) models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As a result, predictions for unknown or out-of-domain data are incorrectly reported as highly likely by the model. To overcome this shortcoming, a novel $p_{\text{open-world}}$ function is proposed, extending the softmax format to model the unknown category. The proposed open-world uncertainty model is trained via an energy-based minimization framework that combines contrastive learning with a sample selection mechanism. This results in a more plausible probability distribution than the conventional softmax format, as evaluated through both quantitative and qualitative methods. The proposed approach outperforms existing calibration techniques, with execution efficiency allowing it to be applied to real-world applications. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The framework is highly adaptable and adaptable, making it suitable for a broad spectrum of lifelong learning applications, from multi-task learning to continuous learning in dynamic environments. The code for the environment, associated experiments, and evaluation tools is available at https://github.com/MLReasearch/FaradayBench, and further details on L2Explorer can be found at https://www.faradaybench.org/detail?name=L2Explorer. The environment is available for download at https://www.dropbox.com/s/clg3gaxgxxeh3za/l2explorer.zip?dl=0. The final version of this manuscript is submitted to the journal Machine Learning: Science and Systems (MLJ), and we are pleased to share that it has been accepted and will be presented at the 2023 Conference of the annual Conference of the International Conference on Machine Learning. The presentation can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q5x5Q5x5Q5x. The environment's primary learning agent is based on the Rlkit.pytorch framework, and the code for the environment itself is written in C#, utilizing the Unity game engine. The project also incorporates a range of popular libraries, including Pytorch, Numpy, and Scipy. In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances. Furthermore, we observe that the delocalized state can be achieved experimentally without highly precise placement of defects, providing a basis for the development of wave propagation applications across long distances in one dimension. Conversely, localized states can undergo a transition to non-localized states with the application of an external electric field in atomic or molecular systems, potentially offering a pathway for the precise placement of defects in future experiments. Finally, our findings suggest that electronic systems with a high degree of freedom may exhibit more complex behavior under similar conditions. The delocalized state in these systems can be understood through a representation of intrinsically interacting particles that form bound pairs that maintain their identity over extended distances, potentially giving rise to more complex phenomena under these conditions. The name "reentrant transition" is also applicable to these systems. The theoretical model used was the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a periodic potential that represents the quasiperiodic modulation of the dielectric constant. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. We explore various conditions under which this improved performance can be achieved, and the associated information gain may be applied to estimate unknown parameters of the system. The novel strategy presented here facilitates the optimal utilization of SpaDE in scenarios involving weak light sources, thereby offering a level of performance beyond what standard techniques can achieve. The approach is experimentally validated using a computer-generated absorption grid equivalent to that in our experimental setup, consisting of a 0.6 mm-diameter pinhole positioned 100 cm from the source. The associated data and analysis are available at https://github.com/leonardoconti/SPADE-supres-resolution-experiments, providing a framework for the thorough examination of our results. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. The corresponding results from numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions. The model used in this study is a modification of a three-level ecosystem model previously presented by Arino et al. [1], and the new results obtained provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's behavior near the singular Hopf point. The model exhibits a similar bifurcation structure to certain ecosystem models described by Arino et al. and Mallet-Yaque et al. [2], and the early warning signs detected in this study may be applicable to those models as well. The underlying dynamics of these models rely on a two-timescale structure, and the results obtained suggest that the mechanism behind a regime shift in these models is a combination of the singular Hopf bifurcation and the resulting mixed-mode oscillations. The conditions derived for the model used in this study may serve as a basis for developing a more general theory for predicting early warning signs in a broader class of ecosystem models. The models considered in this study are not directly applicable to the models presented by Cottle and Lebowitz [3] and Lebowitz and Cottle [4], which involve different time scales, but the results obtained may be relevant to a time-scale reassignment of the Cottle-Lebowitz model. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern mirrors the decline in blue galaxies above this mass threshold, suggesting a complete shift in galaxy behavior at this point. It is here that bulge growth dominates, resulting in a dip in the star-forming main sequence at the high mass end. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The obtained outcomes suggest that program correctness preservation holds important implications for program behavior, while program performance is largely influenced by the specific coherence protocol and particular program workloads. The devised technique for optimal fence insertion proves very efficient in ensuring program correctness but tends to generate programs with higher overhead compared to baseline programs. In contrast, the simplified fence insertion procedure developed in this research yields more practical outcomes, especially considering the relatively low overhead when compared to other coherence protocols. The prototype implementation highlights the potential benefits of counter-example driven optimization methods, which facilitate the rapid discovery of effective solutions, although more efficient ones may exist. The challenge of optimal fence insertion remains a topic for further exploration, mainly in light of the recent breakthroughs achieved. The formaly verified optimality of a given solution suggests that future protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade may employ a combined approach, incorporating multiple coherence protocols, to ensure program correctness. The associated code can be found at the link: https://github.com/abhishek431/fence-verification. The formal framework for programs operating under a combined protocol was formally presented at the conference. The associated code can be found at the link: https://github.com/abhishek431/combined-verification. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable. The findings are supported by both spectral analysis and numerical simulations. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. This discovery may provide valuable insights into the evolutionary pathways of intermediate mass stars or offer a chance to explore new physical processes within these stars. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of conducting detailed internal stellar rotations analyses through a combination of space and ground-based observations. This study also highlights the importance of evaluating candidate exoplanets' presence through various methods, such as light curve analysis, radial velocity measurements, and direct visual inspection, before drawing conclusions about the presence or absence of these planets. Lastly, it emphasizes that future observations should consider accounting for any detected irregular pulsational patterns when interpreting stellar evolution markers. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The evaluation results show that the proposed system performs well when there is sufficient supporting evidence but is particularly strong in detecting false information when there is limited supporting evidence. The source code of the MetaFEND system has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/seyedmohammadghasemi/MetaFEND. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the radiation field's Wigner function from a state reconstruction process. We examine the feasibility of directly inferring the Wigner function from an overcomplete set of tomographic states, without first reconstructing the system's density operator. We demonstrate this ability for coherent and number states, and even with homodyne detectors set to specific tomographic angles, we can derive the phase space distribution directly. Furthermore, we investigate the application of this approach to analyzing entanglement and synchronization in multi-mode systems. In such systems, reconstructing the density operator becomes an even more intricate process, often involving multiple measurements with different tomographic states. We show that when the system involves multiple modes, even with homodyne detectors set to specific tomographic angles, we can derive the Wigner function and infer the presence of entanglement, but not synchronization. Furthermore, we discuss the applicability of this approach for discussing multi-mode entanglement in systems where the number of modes is unknown, without first knowing the system's density operator. We explore the feasibility of directly deriving the Wigner function using a different set of tomographic states that are orthogonal to those used for the measurements. We used numerical simulations to analyze a system of up to three harmonic oscillators, and demonstrated that their density operators can be accurately described using an overcomplete set of tomographic states, thus allowing the derivation of their Wigner function through a kind of variational approach. We also examined the limitations of this approach by applying it to systems that exhibit synchronization, and found that while it can handle a a system of up to two harmonic oscillators accurately describing its density operator, it fails when one of the oscillators is a spin system. Conversely, it succeeds when the other oscillator is a spin system but fails with a system of three harmonic oscillators when two of the oscillators are entangled. We attribute these failures to the presence of either classical or quantum correlations within these systems, and we believe that this approach has the potential to overcome these challenges. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this goal involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. Human
evaluators also found the systems plausible and engaging. We believe that our
approach may facilitate development of more adaptable and role-aware open-domain
dialogue systems. The data collection methods and role-compliant dialogue models
we introduced may be applied to other context-rich text generation tasks as well. The code and data are available at: https://github.com/strmlab/role-specified-open-domain-dIALOGUE. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, the model's effectiveness is further validated
by testing it with actual viewer data obtained from real streaming scenarios.

25%, indicating the significant contribution of video subtitles in improving
the model's performance. The proposed model's precision in predicting user views

parts of the viewing area, whereas the accuracy drops to 50% when some parts
of the viewing area contain less prominent objects. Moreover, the model's
performance is not significantly affected by videos featuring up to 10 objects
within the viewing area. Nevertheless, the model's primary limitation is its
dependence on accurately translated subtitles, which, if incorrect, may lead to
a decline in the model's precision. The model's reliance on such additional

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, last from milliseconds to several hundred seconds. Although they seem random, glitches occur more frequently during specific satellite movements, known as the S-shaped regime. This occurrence is believed to result from interactions between the satellite's radiation shield and the test masses. A statistical analysis of these events was used to develop a model that predicts their likelihood, based on the time it takes the satellite to complete one orbit and its movement within that orbit. This model can be used to update the estimated testing error for the weak equivalence principle test. Given the frequency of glitches in the Microscope data, it's clear that they could pose a significant threat to the accuracy of this test, potentially exceeding the planned testing error for certain violation patterns. This discovery is significant, as it highlights the importance of understanding and accounting for glitches when interpreting the results of this test. This time-based approach to analyzing these events can also be applied to other gravitational physics experiments conducted in orbit. In the context of the Microscope test, it's essential to control glitches through appropriate data processing methods or shielding techniques, as the natural environment of space, combined with the limitations of hardware, will always present a level of glitch-induced threat to this type of experiment. Therefore, the development of sensitive gravitational physics experiments in the future should prioritize the design of robust hardware that can effectively handle the presence of glitches in space. This will involve creating hardware that can operate with a minimal glitch impact, coupled with a sophisticated data processing system that employs a statistical approach to identifying and excluding unreliable measurement data. This will be a critical aspect to consider in the development of the Tino experiment, a next-generation Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle, which will face similar environmental challenges and likely face similar glitches. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree. Specifically, we establish that the frog model is recurrent if the frog population size exceeds the degree of the tree, and it is transient if the population size is less than the degree, although there may be an exceptional population size that also results in a transient state. Additionally, we show that this transition is sharp by examining the underlying conditions and proof methods used for trees. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. A general approach is described for converting an SG instance into an equivalent 3-Clique finding problem, although the general version of this problem was found to have an unacceptably high parameterization, suggesting further study is needed on SG in graph classes defined by specific structural properties. The research described may serve as a foundation for further exploration and the development of more efficient, general algorithms addressing SG in various graph types. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. The code is available at https://github.com/google-research/trail. The paper extends previous work on transition-based models by incorporating external feedback, and the results show that using such models can lead to a 4x performance gain on difficult tasks. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Key advantages of CoIL include optimized expert data usage and minimized policy instability compared to traditional methods. Moreover, our approach showcases robust performance across various exploration settings and a notable ability to mitigate over-exploration. In line with stateful reinforcement learning principles, our method achieves results that improve over time, showcasing a notable time-dependent achievement ramp-up effect. The innovative Co-Imitation Learning framework is made available through our open-source repository. Our research provides a groundbreaking solution to the long-standing challenge of reinforcing learning without relying on external expert guidance. The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
These advancements pave the way for utilizing systems that are out of equilibrium 
to develop novel technologies such as robust quantum clocks and secure quantum 
communication networks. 
Additionally, we propose a hybrid use of different types of driving forces, 
such as laser pulses and environmental influences, that could provide even 
greater control over the system's steady state.
Our research also reveals that the disordered state of the system can be maintained 
by reversing the flow of energy at regular intervals, a feature that could be 
useful in developing lossless quantum clocks.
Furthermore, we illustrate that the system's steady state can be designed to function 
as a secure channel for quantum communication by preventing any loss of information 
and restricting access to a specific group of observers. 
Lastly, we discuss the implications of our research, highlighting the importance 
of considering the system's surroundings and the periodic driving forces.
Our open system can be replicated using a wide range of systems, such as spin systems 
and superconducting circuits, and our research provides a theoretical framework 
that could be applied to developing novel technologies in the laboratory. 
However, our study also raises fundamental concerns about the system's stability

forces and environmental influences are consistent with the requirements set by

interactions with its surroundings.

Our findings are particularly applied to identify specific characteristics of biharmonic hypersurfaces when these operators result in a minimal or stable outcome. Moreover, our research provides a comprehensive framework for a substantial number of previously known and newly derived theorems and conclusions related to biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space. A new set of axiomatic operators called 'biharmonic operators' is also introduced, along with a related classification that further elaborates on how these operators impact biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space. A key aspect of our proof relies on a newly formulated 'biharmonic functional equation' that provides a comprehensive explanation for a hypersurface being biharmonic whenever its geometric structure is analyzed within the Euclidean space. A key contribution of this research is the introduction of a set of 'biharmonic operator conditions' that can be applied to a broad category of operators such as curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators, or any other operator that can be defined using a set of given properties. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. The total DM density within the model is determined by adding the contributions from these various processes. It is found that the model can accommodate a wide range of mass spectra for both the axion and sterile-neutrino components. Furthermore, we are able to identify specific regions within the parameter space that comply with the constraints imposed by both observational data and laboratory experiments. The model also predicts the existence of a very low-mass component within the solar system, comprised of about $10^{12}$ axions, and suggests a possible connection between the neutrino properties and the properties of the universe on a cosmological scale. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. We hope our work will be useful not only for validating the correctness of MongoDB's transaction protocols but also for providing a useful example for the formal verification of complex, real-world protocols. While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Our research provides a starting point for the development of more advanced methods that can locate and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets,, potentially allowing for the design of more effective debiasing techniques.  Our work is also relevant to the broader field of machine learning dataset selection,,, potentially enabling the selection of low-bias datasets for medical image analysis tasks. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. The average power loss due to radiative cooling was about 50 Watts per square meter, and the net heat gain from solar photons was around 140 Watts per square meter, which left us with some interesting questions about the overall energy dynamics within the solar corona. The relationships we identified may not remain the same in areas of the corona where plasma is unstable or where magnetic fields are strong enough to hinder the free flow of solar winds, and future missions will need to consider visiting locations even closer to the solar surface. The data also highlighted the significant impact that extremely low frequency variations in the solar wind's energy flux could have on the overall energy flux observed over short periods, and it may be beneficial to either record data over longer periods or at times of minimal variation for more accurate representations of the normal behavior of solar wind energy flux. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  We propose a relation between structural changes, electronic pressure and the spin polarization pressure to explain these magnetic alterations or loss.  These findings highlight NFS capability in magnetism detection within complex materials under high pressure and temperature conditions.  We suggest that NFS employ multiple detectors or distribution analysis to derive more accurate magnetic results.  Additionally, we observe pressure-induced changes in the NFS distribution, suggesting a change in the magnetic correlation length, and propose studying this in greater detail in future studies.  Our results demonstrate that NFS offers a distributive, model-independent approach for studying magnetic alterations under high pressure and temperature conditions, providing valuable insights into the structure-property relations of complex materials.  We anticipate that this will lead to a renewed interest in this technique, leading to the development of new experiments and theoretical models.  Finally, we believe that NFS will continue to play a crucial role in the study of materials under high pressure and temperature conditions, and we look forward to seeing the results of future studies in this field. Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Increasing the radius of the void's edge while keeping the index constant results in increased compression and heating within the layer, leading to a more abrupt transition in both models and further evidence for self-similar behavior in this scenario. Similarities in both solutions suggest that the area where the inner edge's density becomes infinite at approximately 1.4 may hold significant physical importance. Additionally, when the index is greater than 1.4, a singular unstable configuration emerges, while in contrast, a uniform, stationary, infinite density at the origin constitutes a new stable solution with an index of 1.4. An analysis of stability using a small perturbation shows that when the index is between 1.4 and 1.5, the singular configuration can be restored through a periodic oscillation in the layer, resulting in a void with periodic walls. An analysis of this scenario suggests that when the index lies between 1.4 and 1.5, multiple solutions could exist, and all of them could be found along the line that connects the points (0, 1.4) and (1, 1.5) on the adiabatic index graph. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. The tool's capabilities are demonstrated by analysing the impact of instrumental systematic effects on recovering the cosmic microwave background anisotropy signal in data similar to those expected from the CMB-S4 experiment. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, it identifies additional desirable properties of the Euclidean space structure, which include the existence of straight lines and the property of angle preservation, which it achieves by introducing the notion of an angle-preserving mapping. Ultimately, this article demonstrates that any metric space with the property of betweenness can be embedded isomorphically onto a subspace of a Euclidean space, specifically a subspace defined by the set of all straight lines that have a non-empty intersection with that space. This solution to Menger's problems essentially relies on the advanced tools of category theory and the methodology of internal logic, which are introduced in an appendix of this article for the benefit of researchers who may not be familiar with these advanced mathematical techniques. This article hopes to provide a comprehensive exploration of the potential applications of the theory of angle functions across various disciplines and fields of study. Additionally, it provides a more general definition of the property of betweenness, which it applies not just to metric spaces but also to semi-metric spaces, relation spaces, and even philosophical concepts of nearness and closeness. We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy and stability. Specifically, it allows for precise measurements of pressure (CFM<1.2), temperature (T<600 K) and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios (O2/N2) in a single shot. We demonstrate its effectiveness in measuring gas properties within small cells (1 cm3), as well as in larger environments (20 cm3), resulting in the creation of a pressure map in a cubic volume 5 cm in length. Additionally, we explore the scope of this method by applying it to the analysis of a vibrating cylinder in a pressurized environment and observe the propagation of a pressure wave in a pressurized gas and the mixing of gases in a ratio of 1:1, 1:3 and 3:1. This technique holds great promise for the development of advanced, non-invasive pressure sensing technologies. By incorporating a spiral probe, it may also enable the creation of compact, portable and high-performance pressure sensors. Furthermore, we examine the potential of this technique to be adapted for the analysis of biological samples in a living state. Although further work is needed to fully explore its applications in this field, it is clear that this method offers a groundbreaking approach to the multidisciplinary study of mechanical biology. 
  In correspondence with our previous paper, we include a numerical solution to the time-domain measurement equation, in addition to the implementation of a wave propagation model that integrates pressure and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratio measurements. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. This is particularly significant in applications involving large-scale decentralized learning across graphs, across multiple classes, and with varying network topologies. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By exploring Forsage's behavior and outcomes for over 400,000 participants across 177 countries, the study reveals the scheme's intricate structure and the devastating consequences it had for the majority of its users. The data highlights the typical pyramid characteristics of Forsage, with users at the base consistently losing money to those above them, while a small group of top participants made significant profits. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, valid for transverse momenta above mass thresholds, to describe exclusive Drell-Yan processes involving heavy quarks within jets. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Further analysis of ablation studies and model evaluations highlights the benefits of sparse representations in enhancing generative performance. We anticipate that future text generation models integrating sparse coding will lead to further breakthroughs in modeling complex linguistic hierarchies. Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Consequently, joint modeling of resource selection and capture-recapture data offers a compelling approach to investigating the complex interplay between animals' population size, resource selection, and spatial behavior. Furthermore, we recommend the use of a reliability index for model-averaged density estimates to account for the relative precision of each model.
