Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. We discover that certain sound classes are more challenging to localize than others and propose a theoretical model explaining the factors influencing localizability. This model highlights the importance of identifying the visual features characteristic of certain sounds and the role of ambient sounds in the video frame. Moreover, we propose a novel framework called the Visual Sound Source Tree (VSS-T), a hierarchical representation of sound sources that complements existing audio descriptors, such as Fourier magnitude spectra and Convolutional Neural Network feature vectors. Finally, we explore the VSS-T's usability as a labeling tool and its potential to facilitate the manual annotation of sound sources within video data. This tool's interface is similar to popular image annotation interfaces, such as VGG Annotator, yet tailored to sound source labeling, driven by the unique characteristics of visual sound data. Additionally, we introduce an interactive method called SoundSourceRank (SSRANK) that ranks sound sources within video frames based on user input, such that the most difficult sound sources are prioritized first. This algorithm's effectiveness is validated through a user study involving multiple participants. Lastly, we examine the potential applications of our research in the context of artificial intelligence, specifically sound-based object detection, across domains such as robotics and the visual sound domain, and explore the concept of a Flickr SoundNet-style dataset tailored to video data. This theoretical framework for such a dataset is called the Visual Sound Domain Hierarchy (VSDH). Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective in representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. The implementation of LGCN is made available to the public. Moreover, a comparative analysis of LGCN with existing methods is provided, along with a practical application showcasing LGCN's capabilities. This includes a case study where LGCN is employed to categorize hidden nodes in a molecular graph derived from the NCI dataset. The results indicate that LGCN excels in relational reasoning tasks, particularly those involving hierarchical, small-scale datasets. The source code of the experiment is made available online. Moreover, a set of hyperparameter tuning experiments is conducted and the optimized parameter settings are included alongside the code. The effectiveness of LGCN is further validated through a simplicity and effectiveness perspective, and it is observed that LGCN's simplicity of design directly contributes to its superior performance. This includes a discussion on why LGCN's operations are effective, and it is argued that LGCN's success can be attributed to its adherence to the underlying geometry of graph data, and that this approach may also be applicable to other exotic geometric domains. The scope of future work on this topic is also outlined, and this involves exploring LGCN on larger-scale datasets, the integration of LGCN with other graph-based methods, and a more in-depth examination of LGCN's performance in tasks involving hierarchical data. The name "Lorentzian graph convolutional network" is proposed for this method, and it is shown that this approach outperforms all existing state-of-the-art

This discovery may lead to the development of phonon-squeezed state-producing devices in optomechanical form. Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this report provides a discussion on the experimental verification of negative temperature, including a review of recent experiments verifying negative absolute temperature in both classical and quantum systems. Finally, an attempt is made to provide a critical perspective on the implementation of negative temperature within a variety of applications, along with a commentary on the often-hyped media coverage of such topics. We hope this report can serve as an engaging and informative discussion on negative absolute temperature that can be utilized in lectures or seminars. Additionally, the report includes an accompanying spreadsheet that can be used for interactive calculations. The spreadsheet is readily available for download from the associated website. We believe that combining theoretical calculations with experimental evidence, along with a critical perspective on the implementation of negative temperature, can provide an enjoyable and enlightening experience for both undergraduate students and academics alike. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. UniToPatho is unique in its comprehensive scope, addressing not just polyp detection but also dysplasia assessment, thereby filling a significant gap in currently available datasets. To facilitate seamless integration into existing research, we've established a framework comprising three distinct subsets of annotated patches, along with corresponding classification and grading metrics. This dataset, hosted on a publicly accessible platform, is also accompanied by a technical report outlining UniToPatho's construction, comprising a multi-step process involving polyp location, characterizing and grading, followed by automatic patch extraction. The development of this dataset is a collaborative effort between pathologists, clinicians, and researchers, with expert input ensuring the accuracy and reliability of annotations. UniToPatho is well-suited for evaluating the efficacy of deep learning-based approaches targeting colorectal polyp detection, characterization, and grading. We've conducted a preliminary assessment of this dataset's performance, achieving notable results with a state-of-the-art deep learning model that demonstrated exceptional characterization and grading accuracy. Nonetheless, there is ample scope for further improvement, as UniToPatho is but a starting point for the challenging task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. We strongly advocate the use of UniToPatho as a benchmark for evaluating the grasp of current computer vision techniques on this complex subject matter, with opportunities for meaningful contributions that will, in turn, push the boundaries of further advancements. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Our findings also indicate that zero-shot speech-to-text models often outperform two-stage baselines, with results indicating that speech translation datasets prove useful for related zero-shot translation pairs. Our analysis demonstrates zero-shot speech-to-text's potential to tackle underrepresented languages and necessitates the development of more flexible models capable of managing non-standard dialects.
